title: Zechariah
subtitle: eight night visions, a crowned priest, and a question about fasting
lead: Zechariah is the longest of the Twelve Minor Prophets (211 verses) and one of the most quoted in the New Testament. It begins in 520 BC, in the same small Persian province and the same weeks as Haggai. A prophet, Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, tells the people who are rebuilding the Temple to turn back to the LORD. Then, on one night in February 519, he sees eight visions: riders who have walked the earth, four horns and four craftsmen, a man measuring Jerusalem, the high priest Joshua cleansed in front of the Accuser, a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, a flying scroll, a woman sealed in a basket, and four chariots. An angel explains each. Crowns are made and set on Joshua's head, and nearly two years later a delegation asks whether the fasts that mourned the Temple should continue. The answer ends the first half: the fasts will become feasts, and the nations will come to Jerusalem.

The second half (chapters 9-14) has no dates and no name for its author. It is made of two oracles, each headed "oracle" (9:1; 12:1), and contains some of the passages the Gospels use most: the king who comes on a donkey, the thirty pieces of silver, the one they pierced, the shepherd who is struck, and the day when the LORD's feet stand on the Mount of Olives. Its date, its author and its relation to chapters 1-8 are among the most argued questions in the study of the Prophets. This site gives chapters 1-8 and chapters 9-14 as two parts of one book, with the question of unity set out below.
facts: Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo (1:1, 7), a prophet and probably a priest, since Nehemiah 12:16 lists a Zechariah as head of Iddo's priestly house. Chapters 9-14 are anonymous; whether the same prophet wrote them is debated (see "Who wrote Zechariah?").

Chapters 1-8 carry three dates in the reign of Darius I: the eighth month of his second year (late October to late November 520 BC, 1:1), the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month (15 February 519, 1:7) and the fourth day of the ninth month of his fourth year (7 December 518, 7:1). The book was shaped soon after, or later in the Persian period. Chapters 9-14 are undated; a Persian-period or Greek-period setting is argued.

Jerusalem and the province of Judah (Hebrew Yehud) in the Persian Empire, during the rebuilding of the Temple under the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua (finished in Darius's sixth year, about 516-515 BC, Ezra 6:15).

Chapters 1-8: prose reports of visions in a fixed pattern (the prophet sees, asks "What is this?", an angel explains), with oracles, a sign act and an exchange about fasting. Chapters 9-14: two oracles, mixing poetry and prose, with no dates. The repeated phrases are "the angel who spoke with me," "I looked up and saw," "The LORD of Armies says this," and "Then you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me."
Hebrew, with a few words from Babylonian (the month names Shebat and Kislev) and rare words such as tsanif ("turban") and mahlekhim ("places to walk").
14 chapters, 211 verses (21, 13, 10, 14, 11, 15, 14, 23, 17, 12, 17, 14, 9, 21): chapters 1-8 have 121 verses and chapters 9-14 have 90.

English and Hebrew agree except at the start of the book: English 1:18-21 is Hebrew 2:1-4, so the Hebrew chapter 2 begins at English 1:18 and runs to English 2:13 (Hebrew 2:1-17; only English 2:1-13 equal Hebrew 2:5-17), and the Hebrew chapter 1 has 17 verses. Hebrew Zechariah also has 14 chapters and 211 verses. The Greek (Swete's text) follows the Hebrew numbering. This site uses the English numbers.

The eleventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in both the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi) and the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi). With Haggai and Malachi it is one of the three post-exilic prophets.

History (H), Critical (C), Jewish tradition (J), Christian (X) and Still to come (F) apply to the whole book. F matters most for chapters 9-14, the coming king, the shepherd and the day of the LORD, and in chapters 1-8 for the Branch (3:8-10; 6:12-15) and the nations' pilgrimage (2:10-11; 8:20-23).
authorship: Zechariah the prophet wrote or spoke the whole book. Jewish tradition counts the Twelve as one book written by the Men of the Great Assembly (Bava Batra 15a), and counts Zechariah with Haggai and Malachi among the last prophets (Yoma 9b). Ben Sira, about 180 BC, names "the twelve prophets" right after Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel and prays, "And may the bones of the twelve prophets sprout again from their place" (Sirach 49:10). Christian writers from the Fathers on took all fourteen chapters as one prophet's, and the Gospels quote chapters 9-14 as Scripture without naming Zechariah as the author: Matthew 21:4-5 says "through the prophet," Matthew 26:31, Mark 14:27 and John 12:15 say "it is written," John 19:37 says "another Scripture," and Matthew 27:9-10 names Jeremiah for a quotation that includes Zechariah 11:12-13. (Matthew 23:35 names a Zechariah son of Berechiah, but for a murder and not for these chapters.)

Most critical scholars assign chapters 1-8 to Zechariah, and chapters 9-14 to later anonymous writers, usually in two blocks (9-11 and 12-14), each headed "oracle" like the opening of Malachi (1:1). The argument began in the seventeenth century with Joseph Mede, who noticed that Matthew 27:9 names Jeremiah for a verse in Zechariah 11 and suggested that chapters 9-11 were Jeremiah's; Hitzig then placed chapters 12-14 under another author, in the time of Manasseh, and Stade (1881-82) argued that 9-14 came from one writer no earlier than about 300 BC. The names Proto-, Deutero- and Trito-Zechariah (chapters 1-8, 9-11 and 12-14) come from this debate. Reasons given: no dates or names in 9-14, a different style and subject (no visions, no Zerubbabel or Joshua, a fixed 'in that day' idiom), and the mention of Greece (9:13). Scholars who hold this view differ over the dates (Persian or Greek) and over how 9-14 came to stand with 1-8. Boda, for example, treats 1-8 and 9-14 as separately compiled works, with 9-14 joined to an already existing 1-8.

Some scholars defend the unity of the book. Boda, who sees 1-8 and 9-14 as separately compiled and joined early, still reads Zechariah 1-14 as one book. The Plain, notes and cards treat the question as open and mark each reading.

audience.to: Chapters 1-8: the people of the small Persian province of Judah, at the start of the second Temple project: the governor Zerubbabel (a grandson of King Jehoiachin), the high priest Joshua, the priests, the builders and the people of Jerusalem and its villages. A delegation from Bethel asks the 'house' priests and prophets about fasting (7:1-3). The first readers, if the book was shaped later, were Judeans of the Persian period who knew the finished Temple. Chapters 9-14: a community that is not named; the 'shepherds' of the people, Jerusalem and Judah, and the nations around them.
audience.why: To keep the Temple work moving and to say what it is for. The visions tell a poor and anxious province that the LORD has come back to Jerusalem, that its priesthood is cleansed by his decision and not by its record, that it will be fed by his Spirit and not by an army, that wickedness will be removed from the land, and that the nations will one day join them. The prophet's call to justice and truth (7:9-10; 8:16-17) answers the question about fasting: what the LORD wanted was never the fast. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the book is not a timetable of the end, and its figures (Joshua, the Branch, the two sons of fresh oil) first belong to a particular building site in 519 BC.
views: The common view: chapters 1-8 were first for the builders of 520-518 BC. Meyers and Meyers tie Haggai and Zechariah 1-8 to the rededication of the Temple in 515 BC.
Critical scholars place the audience of 9-14 in the later Persian or the Greek period, with a community suffering under foreign rule and leaders called shepherds; they differ on where and when.
Some conservative commentators hold that the whole book is for the community of Zechariah's lifetime, with 9-14 reaching forward to the Messiah and the end.
Read in the synagogue and the church
The Jewish lectionary reads Zechariah 2:14-4:7 (Hebrew numbers) on the Sabbath of Hanukkah and chapter 14 at Booths; the church reads the Branch and the king on the donkey at Advent and Palm Sunday.

outline: A call to turn back: "Return to me, and I will return to you"
Vision 1: the riders among the myrtle trees
Vision 2: four horns and four craftsmen
Vision 3: the man with the measuring cord, and the call from Babylon
Vision 4: Joshua, the Accuser and the Branch
Vision 5: the lampstand, the two olive trees and Zerubbabel
Vision 7: the woman in the ephah
The crowning of Joshua and the word about the Branch
The question about fasting and the lesson of the earlier prophets
Ten sayings: the LORD returns, the fasts become feasts, the nations come
First oracle: judgment on Hadrach, Damascus, Tyre and Philistia
The humble king, the prisoners of hope, the LORD's arrow
Shepherds and idols; the LORD cares for his flock
The three shepherds, the staffs Favor and Union, the thirty pieces of silver
Second oracle: Jerusalem delivered, the one they pierced, the fountain, the end of idols and prophets
The shepherd struck and the refining of a third
The day of the LORD: the feet on the Mount of Olives, living water, one LORD, Booths

lenses.name: History
lenses.desc: Reads the book against the Persian period: Darius I in 520-518 BC, the province of Yehud, Zerubbabel and Joshua, the building of the Temple (finished in Darius's sixth year), and the fasts for 586. For chapters 9-14 it asks which events fit: Alexander's march, the Persian or Greek period, or an earlier date.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made: how the visions and oracles were joined, whether chapters 9-14 are by another hand (Proto-, Deutero- and Trito-Zechariah), whether the crowning of Joshua replaced Zerubbabel, what the Greek and the Dead Sea scrolls (4Q80, Mur88) show, and how the Accuser and the Branch developed.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Zechariah as Jews have read it: the Targum (which reads the Branch as the Messiah), the Talmud on the four craftsmen (Sukkah 52b), the fast days (Rosh Hashanah 18b), the Hanukkah and Booths haftarot (Megillah 31a), and Maimonides on the Messiah building the Temple.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Zechariah as the church has: the Branch and the Dawn (Luke 1:78), Joshua as a picture of Jesus (Justin), the lampstand and olive trees in Revelation 11:4, the king on the donkey (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15), the thirty pieces (Matthew 27:9-10), the pierced one (John 19:37; Revelation 1:7) and the struck shepherd (Matthew 26:31), with Calvin's lectures on Zechariah.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Used for passages read as not yet fulfilled: in chapters 1-8 the Branch's coming and the single day of cleansing (3:8-10), the building of the temple by the Branch (6:12-15), the nations' pilgrimage (2:10-11; 8:20-23); in chapters 9-14 the coming king, the shepherd and the day of the LORD. Dispensationalist, premillennial, amillennial, preterist and Jewish readings differ.

sections.b:
Read the first half as a conversation. A prophet speaks to a people who are building a Temple, who are poor, doubtful and surrounded by a calm that looks like the LORD's silence. The eight visions come as one night's answer to "How long?" (1:12). Each follows the same steps: the prophet looks up and sees, asks "What is this?" and an angel explains. The angel is "the angel who spoke with me" throughout, and the Plain keeps that English every time. The visions are arranged in a ring: horses (1:8) open the series and chariots (6:1) close it; the earth is quiet at the start (1:11) and the LORD's spirit is at rest in the north at the end (6:8). In the middle are the cleansing of the priest (3) and the lampstand fed by the LORD (4).

Chapters 7-8 are different: a question about fasts, and ten sayings in answer. The book's main word returns at the start and the end: "Return to me" (1:3) and "I have turned again" (8:15), "Let us go ... to ask the LORD's favor" (7:2; 8:21-22).

The Plain follows the Bible Scroll's terms. The LORD is YHWH ("the LORD"), YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies," ne'um YHWH is "the LORD declares," koh amar is "says this." The Accuser (hassatan, with the article) is "the Accuser" at 3:1-2, as in Job 1-2, and 1 Chronicles 21:1 (no article) has "Satan." The high priest is "Joshua son of Jehozadak," as in Haggai, who is "Jeshua son of Jozadak" in Ezra and Nehemiah. Tsemach is "the Branch" with a capital B when it is a name (3:8; 6:12). "The angel who spoke with me" and "I looked up and saw" are the same English at every use. Zechariah's "my Spirit" (4:6; 7:12) has a capital S when the LORD speaks of his own Spirit.

English and Hebrew verse numbers differ at one place: English 1:18-21 is Hebrew 2:1-4, so the Hebrew chapter 2 begins at English 1:18 and runs to English 2:13, and the Hebrew chapter 1 has 17 verses. The Greek follows the Hebrew numbering. Everything else is the same in both.

The base text is the Leningrad Codex. The Greek is read in Swete's edition (mainly Codex Vaticanus); the critical editions (Rahlfs-Hanhart; the Goettingen Duodecim Prophetae) were not consulted. The Dead Sea scrolls were read in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription: 4Q80 (4QXIIe) preserves parts of chapters 1-3 and 4-8. In the transcription it mostly differs from the Masoretic Text in spelling (waw and yod), but two places may be more: at 8:6 it seems to read a question marker (hgm, "will it also...?") and at 6:5 it appears to lack the words "after standing before" (the words around the gap are restored, so a gap in the leather is possible). Both come from the transcription alone; the Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve (Mur88) preserves part of 1:1-4. The Greek Minor Prophets scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr) was not used. The Ketiv and Qere differences are spellings except at 4:2 ("he said" or "I said"). The notable Greek differences are: "mountains" for "myrtle trees" (1:8, 10, 11), four horse colors for three (1:8), the horns "broken" (1:21), "holy clouds" (2:13), "sickle" for "scroll" (5:1-2), "their injustice" for "their appearance" (5:6), the names turned into words (6:10, 14), "Rising" for "Branch" (3:8; 6:12), "I dig a pit" for "carve its inscription" (3:9), "going out to stand" for "after standing" (6:5), "take excellence" for "bear majesty" and the priest "at his right" (6:13), "for a psalm" for "a memorial" (6:14), a different 7:2-3, and "five cities" (8:21). Each of these has an entry in the variants.

sections.h: Reception: how the New Testament and the synagogue use Zechariah
sections.b: The Gospels draw on Zechariah more than on any of the other Twelve: the king on the donkey (Zechariah 9:9 in Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15), the shepherd struck (13:7 in Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27), the thirty pieces of silver (11:12-13 in Matthew 27:9-10), the one they pierced (12:10 in John 19:37) and the mourning (12:10 in Revelation 1:7). In chapters 1-8 the Dawn of Luke 1:78 echoes the Greek anatolē for the Branch, Jude 9 echoes 3:2, Revelation 11:4 takes up the lampstand and the olive trees, Revelation 6:1-8 and 7:1 use horses and the four winds, and Ephesians 4:25 quotes 8:16. Judaism reads Zechariah 2:14-4:7 (Hebrew) on the Sabbath of Hanukkah, Zechariah 14 at the festival of Booths and keeps the four fasts of 8:19. Each use is noted at the verse; these are receptions and not what the Hebrew first said. The Calvin readings named in the notes were checked against his lectures on Zechariah (Owen's translation).

The second half is written and noted in a separate part of this site (chapters 9-14). It has the two oracles, the humble king, the three shepherds, the pierced one, the shepherd struck and the day of the LORD. The question of how it relates to chapters 1-8 is set out under "Who wrote Zechariah?" above.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the book of 1-8 moves from "return" to "let us go"
spec.body: My reading is that chapters 1-8 are built on one movement of verbs. The book opens with the LORD's call to the people: "Return to me" (1:3), which fails in the ancestors' case (1:4-6) and succeeds when the LORD himself returns to Jerusalem (1:16; 8:3). It then turns outward: a delegation goes to "ask the LORD's favor" (7:2), and at the end whole cities go to do the same (8:21-22) and ten men from the nations take hold of a Jew's robe to go with him (8:23). The movement is from a people told to turn, to a God who has turned, to nations who go. The single movement of verbs is my own framing.

prompts: The riders among the myrtle trees

A hand-drawn scroll picture in ink and earth colors: a man on a red horse in a dark grove of myrtle trees at night, with reddish-brown and white horses behind him and riders in the shadows. Cave-drawing style horses, soft torn edges like old parchment, no hard rectangle.

A sketch on aged papyrus mixing ancient manuscript style and modern line art: an old priest in filthy clothes standing before a tall angel, a dark accusing figure at his right side, and servants lifting a clean white turban. Soft uneven borders, a few Hebrew letters in the margin.
The lampstand and the two olive trees

A hand-drawn scroll illustration of a golden lampstand with a bowl on top and seven small flames, two olive trees on either side with golden oil running down into the bowl. Ink, ochre and indigo, edges faded like a worn scroll, no hard rectangle.

A sketch in ink and ochre of a large round grain basket with a heavy lead lid, a woman's hand pressed against the inside, and two winged women lifting it between earth and sky over a plain of mud-brick towers. Cave-painting figures, soft ragged edges.
reading: Carol L. Meyers and Eric M. Meyers, Haggai, Zechariah 1-8 (Anchor Bible 25B, 1987)
A full commentary on Haggai and Zechariah 1-8. It argues that the material was prepared for the rededication of the Temple in 515 BC.
David L. Petersen, Haggai and Zechariah 1-8 (Old Testament Library, 1984)
A historical commentary on Haggai and Zechariah 1-8.
Mark J. Boda, The Book of Zechariah (NICOT, 2016)
A full recent commentary on the whole book. It treats 1-8 and 9-14 as separately compiled and joined, and reads the whole as one book.
Joyce G. Baldwin, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi (Tyndale, 1972)
A short Tyndale commentary on the three post-exilic prophets, from a conservative viewpoint.
Paul L. Redditt, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi (New Century Bible, 1995)
A critical commentary in the New Century Bible series.
Wolter H. Rose, Zemah and Zerubbabel (2000)
A study of the Branch and of messianic hope in the early Persian period.
Meredith G. Kline, Glory in Our Midst (2001)
A biblical-theological reading of the night visions.
